meta.source: California Career Technical Education Model Curriculum Standards -- Information and Communication Technologies (ICT) sector, California Department of Education
meta.scope_note: Covers the 11 cross-sector Anchor Standards (common to all 15 CTE industry sectors) plus the Information and Communication Technologies sector's Pathway C, Software and Systems Development -- the pathway that maps to a Python programming course. The ICT sector's other three pathways (A. Information Support and Services, B. Networking, D. Games and Simulation) are not indexed here; add them the same way if this course is ever articulated toward one of them.
meta.alignment_note: No chapter-alignment pass has been run against this framework yet -- every standard below carries carrier: unassigned and tp_chapters: [] as a placeholder, not a finding. Treat that alignment work as a separate, not-yet-scoped pass.

anchor_standards.name: Academics
anchor_standards.paraphrase: Successfully finishing an ICT pathway means meeting the academic standards tied to it, on the way to further education or a job.

anchor_standards.name: Communications
anchor_standards.paraphrase: Working in ICT means using the sector's own vocabulary and communicating clearly, in writing, speech, and multimedia, at a career-ready level.

items.paraphrase: Communication follows a basic model: someone sends a message, someone else receives it.
Communication can break down, and recognizing what gets in the way of a message landing correctly is its own skill.
Reading both what's said and what's implied, then responding appropriately, is part of communicating well.
Clean spelling, grammar, and formatting show up in both written and electronic communication.
The same information often needs to reach different audiences, which means adapting the medium and format each time.
Using digital media and communication tools safely, legally, and responsibly is expected, not optional.
Writing clearly and communicating well, especially with people outside your own background, is its own working skill.
Serving a customer well starts from understanding what a customer-oriented approach actually looks like.

anchor_standards.name: Career Planning and Management
anchor_standards.paraphrase: Making good career decisions means pulling together career information from many different kinds of sources.

items.paraphrase: Knowing your own interests, aptitudes, and skills is the starting point for any real career decision.
Traits like trustworthiness, respect, and responsibility carry real weight in how a career turns out.
Information and communication technologies themselves are tools people use to plan and decide on a career.
Different careers demand different levels of education, training, certification, or licensing, and that's worth researching directly.
A career plan has to account for shifting job trends, social needs, and the economy, not just personal preference.
Professional organizations, industry groups, and labor unions all play a role in how a working society functions.
Small businesses matter to both the California and the global economy.
Employers and colleges increasingly look at a candidate's digital footprint when evaluating them.
A career plan should reflect a person's actual interests, potential pathways, and options after high school.

anchor_standards.name: Technology
anchor_standards.paraphrase: Both existing and brand-new technology get used in the ICT workplace to research and produce information, products, and services.

items.paraphrase: Electronic references are a normal source for gathering information and building products or services.
Technology-based communication tools can help unpack complicated systems and issues, when used responsibly.
More than one source often needs to be pulled together, weighed against each other, and reconciled -- and information and communication technologies are the tools for doing that.
Not all information found digitally is equally trustworthy, and spotting bias or intent in a source matters.
Technology keeps changing, and tracking how it has, does, and will affect a given pathway is worth doing directly.
Different information and communication technologies serve different populations, and choosing the right one is part of the task.

anchor_standards.name: Problem Solving and Critical Thinking
anchor_standards.paraphrase: ICT problems get solved through research, ranging from quick lookups to sustained investigation, using critical and creative thinking.

items.paraphrase: Asking the right question, from more than one point of view, is often the first real step in solving a problem.
Work problems don't always have a predictable shape, and different kinds of reasoning fit different situations.
A complex work environment is a system, and understanding how its parts interact explains its outcomes.
Drawing a sound conclusion from analysis is what actually informs a good decision.
Tracking a problem to its source takes a structured, logical approach, not guesswork.
items.note: chap05's Debugging section traces a symptom back to its structural cause rather than guessing: an indentation error reported at one line but caused by the line above, a decibels bug reported at line 5 but actually on line 4 (integer division). Headers only -- the chapter demonstrates this but doesn't name it as its own skill.

items.paraphrase: Knowing where to look for help solving a problem is itself a resource worth knowing.
Some problems get solved by working through them repeatedly, refining the approach each pass.
items.note: chap07's has_e build-up (inline loop, then encapsulated, then a boolean return, then parameterized) and the incremental construction of uses_any mirror this standard's start-rough-and-refine framing -- the same pattern as AP's 3.9 Developing Algorithms, from the Anchor-standard side.

items.paraphrase: Algorithms are a tool for solving problems, not just an abstract concept.
A large problem becomes tractable once it's broken into smaller components.
items.note: chap03's 'Why functions?' section explicitly frames functions as a way to divide a big program into smaller, debuggable, reusable pieces -- a direct match. chap04's development plan is a literal, numbered decomposition procedure. chap05's recursive decomposition (countdown, the Sierpinski exercise splitting a triangle of degree n into three of degree n-1) is a purer instance of the same idea.

items.paraphrase: Layers of abstraction let you work with a system without tracking every detail underneath it.
items.note: Calling repeat/print_twice without re-deriving what's inside them is a first, light instance of working through a layer of abstraction -- headers only, since the book doesn't use the word 'abstraction' this early and the connection is implicit. chap04's interface/implementation split (two different circle implementations sharing one interface) makes the concept explicit for the first time. chap06's leap of faith -- trusting a function's return value without re-examining its body -- is the clearest, most direct treatment of abstraction in the book so far.

items.paraphrase: Numbers can be represented in more than one base system, including binary and hexadecimal.
Boolean logic underlies both decision-making and searching in computing.
items.note: chap05's boolean expressions and logical operators feed directly into its if statements -- boolean logic driving decision-making is the chapter's structure, not just present in it. chap07's has_e/uses_any (booleans built from in/or) driving linear search, and chap08's re.search result tested against None, are the searching half of the same standard -- the single best new match found in either chapter.

anchor_standards.name: Health and Safety
anchor_standards.paraphrase: ICT work environments come with their own health and safety procedures, and their own specialized vocabulary.

items.paraphrase: Material Safety Data Sheets exist to be located and followed.
Workplace policies and regulations spell out what employers and employees are each responsible for.
Keeping tools, equipment, and supplies stored, clean, and in working order is itself a health and safety practice.
Lifting, bending, and moving equipment safely protects the person doing it.
Preventing and responding to workplace accidents includes understanding ergonomics.
A safe, healthy workplace has to be actively maintained, not just assumed.
OSHA laws and regulations apply to this workplace and are worth knowing.
Maintaining safety and health in the workplace is an ongoing responsibility, restated here as its own point.
E-waste carries health, environmental, and legal risk if it isn't disposed of properly.
Using natural resources like paper and ink deliberately, not wastefully, is a workplace habit.
Conserving energy while computing -- powering down equipment, using power-saving settings -- is a small but real practice.

anchor_standards.name: Responsibility and Flexibility
anchor_standards.paraphrase: Working in the ICT sector means collaborating in ways that show personal and professional responsibility, flexibility, and respect.

items.paraphrase: Financial management choices ripple outward into the economy, the workforce, and the community.
Following through on your role -- whether it's personal, in your community, or at work -- takes real accountability.
Roles and responsibilities shift over time, and adapting to that is part of the job.
Managing time efficiently is what actually lets responsibilities get fulfilled.
High-quality work applies to how a product or presentation is designed, not just built.
Responsible financial management is a skill in its own right, not just a personal habit.
A professional work demeanor includes both behavior and appropriate attire for the field.
Issues with global reach touch the ICT sector too, and documenting that impact is worth doing.

anchor_standards.name: Ethics and Legal Responsibilities
anchor_standards.paraphrase: Professional, ethical, legal behavior means responding thoughtfully to different perspectives and following applicable laws, regulations, and norms.

items.paraphrase: Quality assurance standards exist to be understood and actually put into practice.
Regulatory agencies at every level of government have their own laws and regulations covering this sector.
Ethical, legal practice in ICT means matching the workplace standards the sector has set.
Personal integrity, confidentiality, and ethical behavior matter directly to how a workplace functions.
An organization's culture and practices shape its whole working environment.
Copyright and intellectual property law apply to proprietary information, including how it gets cited.
Confidential information comes with its own rules about who it can be shared with.
Wider technology adoption has brought its own legal and ethical problems, including hacking, scams, and privacy breaches.

anchor_standards.name: Leadership and Teamwork
anchor_standards.paraphrase: Working with peers means engaging with different perspectives, leadership styles, group dynamics, and resolving conflict productively.

items.paraphrase: Good leaders share a recognizable set of responsibilities, competencies, and behaviors.
Successful teams share traits: leadership, cooperation, collaboration, and sound decision-making.
Teamwork, leadership, and citizenship matter in school, community, and workplace settings alike.
Being part of a professional organization, or competing in career-development events, can genuinely sharpen academic preparation and open career doors.
Today's world is interconnected, and that calls for a genuinely global outlook.
Respecting individual and cultural differences is part of valuing diversity in the workplace.
Real ICT-sector problems get solved through active, interactive teamwork.

anchor_standards.name: Technical Knowledge and Skills
anchor_standards.paraphrase: Every pathway in this sector draws on the same core toolkit of hands-on know-how, put into practice by following procedure carefully.

items.paraphrase: The ICT sector has its own terminology and practices worth being able to interpret and explain.
Every corner of the ICT sector comes with its own rules, regulations, and expectations to follow.
Projects and products in this sector have their own specific requirements and expectations to build toward.
Working with industry experts is a real way to gain specific technical knowledge and skill.
Both a single computer and a network are built from hardware and software parts that depend on each other.
Different kinds of information -- text, images, sound, video -- take up different amounts of data, and media formats vary in capacity.
Metric prefixes like kilo, mega, giga, and tera describe scale throughout computing.
Security in computing rests on concepts like authorization, access rights, and encryption.
Industry-standard software -- word processors, spreadsheets, databases, multimedia tools -- are common working tools.
Files get organized and managed within a hierarchical system.
Text, data, sound, video, and images can all move from one software program or system to another, and there's more than one route for doing it.
Different kinds of information call for different search strategies.
Retrieved information should be checked for accuracy, relevance, and completeness.
Online resources can meaningfully support collaboration, research, publishing, communication, and productivity -- or fail to.

anchor_standards.name: Demonstration and Application
anchor_standards.paraphrase: The knowledge and skills named across this sector's anchor and pathway standards get demonstrated directly, in classrooms, labs, and real workplace settings.

items.paraphrase: Work-based learning experiences extend and apply what's learned in the classroom and lab.
Getting genuinely good at a technical pathway is what actually opens the door to certification, licensure, or further study.
Entrepreneurship, self-employment, and new ventures are all real options worth understanding.
Entrepreneurial practices and behaviors apply specifically within ICT-sector opportunities.
A portfolio is one way to show evidence of the skills and knowledge named in these standards.

pathway.name: Software and Systems Development Pathway
pathway.description: Students in this pathway prepare for computer-science-related careers: designing, building, deploying, and maintaining the software systems that keep modern organizations running, from e-commerce to healthcare records to entertainment.

standards.name: Systems Development Process
standards.paraphrase: Building software well means following a real systems-development process, not improvising.

items.paraphrase: A systems-development life cycle moves through recognizable phases: analysis, design, programming, testing, deployment, maintenance, and improvement.
Systems development can follow different models, including a traditional life-cycle approach or agile methods.
Specifications and requirements for a piece of software, new or existing, get developed through a real process.
Working on a development team means operating within that team's defined scope and boundaries.
Versioning is how a project's milestones get tracked over time.
Flowcharts and UML are tools for diagramming a process.

standards.name: Requirements Analysis
standards.paraphrase: Software and systems requirements need to be defined and analyzed before building starts.

items.paraphrase: Development work serves different ends: automating a task, making people more productive, building a model to analyze something, or simply entertaining.
Development work can have unintended consequences -- bugs, security holes, health or environmental risk, privacy problems -- that are worth watching for and preventing.
A development strategy should target what a specific customer actually needs and wants.
Understanding a customer's needs is a distinct analytical step in development.
Requirements and possible solutions both need to be worked out and written down before they can be built.

standards.name: Human-Computer Interfaces
standards.paraphrase: The interface between a person and a piece of technology is itself something to design well.

items.paraphrase: Every interface runs on the same basic cycle: input, processing, output.
A good interface reflects real knowledge of how people think, move, and interact socially.
Accessibility -- for users with disabilities and users who don't speak English -- has to be actively supported, not assumed.

standards.name: Programming Languages
standards.paraphrase: Software gets built in a programming language, and that language sits at some level of abstraction.

items.paraphrase: Programming languages range from low-level, close to the hardware, to high-level and web-based.
Programming languages and protocols interact -- client-side code, server-side code, and a query language reaching into a database are all pieces of the same system.
Software gets built inside some kind of environment -- a simple content editor on one end, a full-featured IDE on the other.
Data has types, and those types get encoded in specific ways.
items.note: chap01 introduces int, float, and str as distinct types with different encodings, and the type() function to check them -- a direct match. chap06's Checking types section (isinstance, a type-guarded factorial) extends it with a second, applied instance -- checking a type at runtime, not just naming types.

items.paraphrase: Programming paradigms differ -- procedural, object-oriented, event-driven, multithreaded -- and each shapes how code gets structured.
Every programming language has its own syntax, and using it correctly matters.
items.note: chap01 introduces syntax errors (missing parentheses, illegal quote marks); chap02's Debugging section explicitly names 'syntax error' as one of three error kinds. Both are about a language's own syntax rules, matching this standard directly.

items.paraphrase: Data structures, arrays, objects, files, and databases are all ways of organizing a program's data.
items.note: chap08's Writing files section (open, read mode vs 'w' mode, close) is a direct match for this standard's 'files' item.

items.paraphrase: Object-oriented programming brings its own vocabulary: objects, properties, methods, inheritance.

A working program leans on a shared toolkit of constructs -- branches and loops, reusable procedures and functions that take parameters, variables to hold state, ways to recover from errors, and sometimes a function that calls itself.
items.note: chap02 introduces variables; chap03 introduces functions, parameters, and the for loop, plus error handling via %%expect. chap04 adds keyword arguments and more parameter work than chapters 2-3 combined. chap05 adds branches (conditionals) and chap06 adds recursion -- 'sometimes a function that calls itself' is this standard's own closing phrase, and chap06's factorial/fibonacci are exactly that. chap07 reinforces variables-holding-state (Updating variables) and a second error-recovery demo. chap08 adds branch-on-condition file-reading loops and TypeError/IndexError recovery. By chapter 8 this standard's full construct list is covered.

items.paraphrase: Different queueing, sorting, and searching algorithms trade off differently against each other.
items.note: chap07's Search section explicitly names and builds the linear-search pattern -- the searching half of this standard. The trade-off half isn't reached; no second search algorithm exists yet to compare it against. Headers only.

items.paraphrase: Development work needs documentation aimed at more than one audience -- comments for other programmers, manuals for users.
items.note: chap02's Comments section is the 'comments for other programmers' half of this standard. chap04's Docstrings section is a more formal instance of the same half -- a documented contract rather than a plain comment, so a distinct but related carrier, not a repeat. The 'manuals for users' half still isn't addressed anywhere.

standards.name: Testing & Debugging
standards.paraphrase: Software has to be tested, debugged, and improved, not just written.

items.paraphrase: Reliable, effective, efficient software shares recognizable characteristics.
A program sometimes has to change because its own specification changed, or because the technology around it moved on.
Code can be optimized deliberately for better performance.
Testing is a distinct step applied to both software and the broader project.
items.note: chap07's Doctest section -- docstring-embedded tests, a dedicated pass/fail vocabulary, and a runner function built for the purpose -- is close to a literal match for testing as its own distinct development step.

items.paraphrase: A finished result gets evaluated against what it was originally required to do.
Debugging is part of quality assurance, not separate from it.
items.note: Every chapter's Debugging section -- same pattern as AP CRD-1.4/CRD-2.I, already the carrier for AP topic 1.4 in every chapter. Headers only throughout; no single chapter's Debugging section is more chapter-specific than any other's.

standards.name: Media Integration
standards.paraphrase: Development projects often pull together more than one kind of media.

items.paraphrase: A print piece, a video, an audio track, and an interactive experience each have their own basic design vocabulary.
Media gets encoded in different ways -- vector versus bitmap graphics, different bit depths -- and each choice trades off differently.
Editing media takes the right tool for the format -- something for animating frame by frame, something for drawing or touching up an image, something for modeling in three dimensions.
A multimedia project -- video, game, interactive site -- moves from storyboard through to finished production.
Choosing a file format and compression level for media is its own analytical decision.
Media has to actually be integrated into a finished project, using the right tools for the job.
A finished project can include media built to a professional standard -- pictures, write-ups, sound, footage -- made or recorded directly rather than borrowed.

standards.name: Web & Online Development
standards.paraphrase: Web and online projects come with their own development process.

items.paraphrase: Web hosting and related services need both server hardware and the right software.
Getting content live online means registering a domain name and arranging both hosting and email for it.
Search engine optimization, including keyword and metadata strategy, is how a site attracts visitors.
E-commerce capability means handling a shopping cart and credit-card transactions, not just listing products.
A website, an online business, or a personal e-portfolio is meant to actually go live, not just stay a plan.
Delivering and retrieving online content quickly is its own optimization problem.

standards.name: Databases
standards.paraphrase: Databases are their own kind of software development.

items.paraphrase: Databases play a critical role in how modern organizations actually function.
Databases are built from basic structures: fields, records, tables, and views.
Tables relate to each other in specific ways -- one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many -- established through primary keys, foreign keys, and indexes.
Data modeling is how a database gets designed around real business needs.
Queries are the tool for extracting and manipulating data, whether selecting it or acting on it.
A well-normalized database follows an appropriate schema.
Moving data between a database and other applications comes with real limitations and challenges.
Turning data into things such as cross-tabulations, graphs, or charts is what actually makes it useful for deciding something.

standards.name: Devices & Robotics
standards.paraphrase: Software gets developed for more than just general-purpose computers, including robotics and other devices.

items.paraphrase: Device-focused development shows up anywhere from personal computers to robots to smart appliances.
Installing equipment and assembling hardware both call for the right tools and testing.
Hardware is what actually captures input, processes it, and acts on it.
Embedded programming involves digital logic, how data is represented at the machine level, and how memory is organized.
A microcontroller can be programmed to run a device or a robot.

standards.name: Intelligent Computing
standards.paraphrase: Intelligent computing is its own area of software development.

items.paraphrase: Models of intelligent behavior raise the question of what actually distinguishes a human from a machine.
Intelligent computing covers areas like perception, proximity sensing, processing, and control.
AI methods include things like neural networks, Bayesian inference, fuzzy logic, and finite state machines.
Making AI behavior actually happen can lean on math-based modeling, reinforcement learning, or probability-based analysis, among other methods.
